title: N-row — ナ ニ ヌ ネ ノ

points.name: ナ
points.explanation: ナ makes the same 'na' sound as hiragana な. Visually, ナ looks remarkably like a capital Roman 'T' rotated slightly, or more precisely: a horizontal stroke crossed by a stroke descending to the lower LEFT. It has two strokes and resembles a simplified 'na' made with just the essential lines. Compare this to the more complex hiragana な, which has four strokes and a loop. ナ appears in ナイフ (knife), ナース (nurse), and ナイト (night / knight). The katakana system's angular simplicity makes many characters like ナ feel very printable and clear.
rules: ナ has two strokes: a horizontal and a stroke descending to the lower left.
Memory: ナ looks like a '+' sign whose upright leans away to the left.

points.name: ニ
points.explanation: ニ makes the same 'ni' sound as hiragana に. Visually, ニ is disarmingly simple — just two horizontal strokes, one shorter above and one longer below, like a Roman numeral II but with different lengths, or a simplified version of the Chinese character 二[に] (two). In fact, this is not a coincidence: katakana ニ was derived from part of a kanji character. ニ appears in ニュース (news), ニット (knit), and ニーズ (needs — as in 'market needs'). The double-horizontal shape makes ニ one of the easiest katakana to write.
rules: ニ = two horizontal strokes. Possibly the simplest katakana character to write.
ニュース (news) uses ニュ — ニ + small ュ = 'nyu'. You'll see ニュース everywhere.
points.flashcardAnswer: ni — same sound as に; looks like two horizontal strokes

points.name: ヌ
points.explanation: ヌ makes the same 'nu' sound as hiragana ぬ. Visually, ヌ has two strokes: a top stroke that runs right and turns down to the left, crossed by a diagonal sweeping to the lower right. Compare this to the very complex hiragana ぬ — ヌ is a dramatic simplification. ヌ is one of the less common katakana characters since the 'nu' sound is relatively rare in English loanwords. The most notable example is ヌードル (noodle), though ヌードル itself is less common than just using the Japanese word うどん or ラーメン.
rules: Same 'nu' as ぬ — 'n' + flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'.
ヌ is a top stroke turning down-left, crossed by a diagonal that sweeps out to the lower right.
ヌ is relatively rare in everyday loanwords — but worth knowing for completeness.

points.name: ネ
points.explanation: ネ makes the same 'ne' sound as hiragana ね. Visually, ネ is a small tick sitting on a horizontal, with a long stroke descending through it and a short diagonal flicking to the lower left — some learners describe it as a 'net' post or a stick figure with a diagonal arm. Four strokes in all. Compare to hiragana ね, which has a complex looping structure. ネ appears in ネクタイ (necktie), ネット (internet / net), and ネイル (nail / nail art). ネイル is particularly useful since nail art is a huge industry in Japan.
rules: ネ is a tick, a horizontal, a long descending stroke and a short diagonal — four strokes total.
ネット (net/internet) and ネクタイ (necktie) are among the most useful ネ words.
points.flashcardAnswer: ne — same sound as ね; looks like a cross with a diagonal stroke

points.name: ノ
points.explanation: ノ makes the same 'no' sound as hiragana の. Visually, ノ is the simplest possible katakana character — just a single stroke sweeping from the upper right down to the lower left. It looks like a slash '/' or a katakana version of the Roman letter 'N' reduced to its most essential diagonal. Compare this to hiragana の, which is a complete loop. ノ appears in ノート (notebook), ノック (knock), and ノイズ (noise). ノート (notebook) is particularly essential for students — it's one of the first words you'd look up as a student in Japan.
rules: ノ = one single stroke, upper right to lower left. The simplest katakana character to write.
ノート (notebook) is essential student vocabulary — もしノートを貸[か]してください is 'Please lend me your notebook'.
points.flashcardAnswer: no — same sound as の; just one diagonal stroke (the simplest katakana!)

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does this katakana make?
chapterPractice.explanation: ニ makes the 'ni' sound — same as hiragana に. It's just two horizontal strokes, making it one of the easiest katakana characters to both read and write.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which hiragana makes the same sound as the katakana ヌ?
chapterPractice.explanation: ヌ and ぬ are both read 'nu'. Katakana and hiragana are two ways of writing the same sounds, so every katakana has a hiragana partner — recognising the pair is what lets you read either script.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ノート (nooto) means 'notebook'. ノ (no) + ー (long o) + ト (to) = nooto. This is essential school vocabulary in Japan — students use ノート constantly for class notes.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ニュース (nyuusu) means 'news'. ニュ (nyu, a combination) + ー (long u) + ス (su) = nyuusu. You'll encounter ニュース constantly — on TV, on apps, in conversation.
